lessons.title: Ask Better Questions
lessons.summary: Open questions invite stories, not one-word answers.

steps.title: Open beats closed
steps.body: “Did you have a good day?” gets “Yeah.” “What was the best bit of your day?” gets a story. Open questions start with what, how or tell me about.

steps.prompt: Open question, or closed?
steps.why: Open questions give people room to share. Closed ones are easy to answer with a single word.

steps.prompt: Open up the question.
steps.why: Starting with “What” invites a description rather than a simple yes or no.

steps.prompt: Which question do you ask most often?
steps.reply: Swapping just that one for something more open can spark much better chats.

steps.body: Ask someone an open question today, starting with “What” or “Tell me about”, and listen to the story.

lessons.title: Follow Up Later
lessons.summary: Asking how something went shows you remembered.

steps.title: Remembering is caring
steps.body: If someone mentions a hospital appointment or a big meeting, asking “How did it go?” afterwards shows you were really listening. It’s one of the simplest ways to feel close.

steps.title: A follow-up message

lines.text: How did your driving test go today?! 🚗

steps.prompt: What’s the best reply?

options.text: Nice.
options.why: A flat reply misses the chance to celebrate the moment with them.

options.text: AMAZING!! So proud of you. How does it feel?
options.why: You celebrated with them and invited them to share more.

options.text: I passed first time too, it’s easy.
options.why: Turning it to yourself takes away from their big moment.

steps.prompt: Your colleague mentioned their mum was having an operation on Tuesday. It’s Wednesday. What’s best?

options.text: Say nothing in case it’s awkward.
options.why: Silence can feel like you didn’t care or forgot.

options.text: “I hope your mum’s op went well. How is she?”
options.why: A gentle follow-up shows you remembered and care.

options.text: Ask everyone else how it went.
options.why: Asking others can feel like gossip rather than care.

steps.prompt: What helps you remember to follow up?
steps.reply: A quick note in your phone can turn good intentions into lovely follow-ups.

steps.body: When someone mentions something coming up, set a reminder to ask how it went.

lessons.title: Ask About Dreams
lessons.summary: Questions about hopes reveal who someone really is.

steps.title: Beyond the to-do list
steps.body: Busy lives make conversations about logistics: dinner, bills, pick-ups. Asking about hopes and dreams, “If you could learn anything, what would it be?”, brings people closer.

steps.prompt: Match the everyday chat to a dream question.

pairs.b: “What would you do with a free year?”

steps.why: Logistics keep life running. Dream questions keep you curious about each other.

steps.prompt: You’re on a long car journey with your dad. What could deepen the chat?

options.text: Put the radio on and stay quiet.
options.why: Easy, but it misses a rare chance for a real talk.

options.text: Ask about the traffic.
options.why: Logistics chat keeps things surface level.

options.text: “What did you dream of doing when you were my age?”
options.why: It invites a story you may never have heard before.

steps.prompt: Who would you love to hear the dreams of?
steps.reply: Lovely. You might be surprised by what you learn.

steps.body: Ask someone close one dream question this week, like “What would you do with a free year?”

lessons.title: Remember the Details
lessons.summary: Small remembered details make people feel truly known.

steps.title: Details say “I see you”
steps.body: Remembering someone’s favourite biscuit, their pet’s name or their tricky colleague tells them you pay attention. These tiny details build a sense of being known.

steps.prompt: A friend once mentioned they love lemon cake. You’re popping round. What’s a lovely touch?

options.text: Bring whatever cake is on offer.
options.why: Kind, but it misses the chance to show you remembered.

options.text: Bring a lemon cake.
options.why: Remembering a small detail shows you really listen.

options.text: Ask them what their favourite cake is again.
options.why: Not bad, but remembering it already feels more special.

steps.prompt: Shows you remembered, or forgot?

cards.text: “Sorry, what does your partner do again?”
“Good luck with your exam on Friday!”
Offering coffee to someone who never drinks it

steps.why: Remembered details make people feel valued. Forgetting is human, but noting details helps.

steps.prompt: Which details do you find easiest to remember?
steps.reply: Lean on that strength, and jot down the rest in your phone if it helps.

steps.body: Note down three small details about someone close, and use one of them this week.

lessons.title: Celebrate Their Wins
lessons.summary: How you react to good news matters as much as bad news.

steps.title: Joy shared is joy doubled
steps.body: When someone shares good news, an excited, curious response, “That’s brilliant! Tell me everything!”, makes them feel closer to you than a quick “Nice.”

steps.title: Good news

lines.text: Guess what? I got the promotion!!

steps.prompt: How do you reply?

options.text: Wow, more stress though?
options.reaction: Oh… I hadn’t thought of that.
options.why: Pointing out downsides dampens her happy moment.

options.text: Cool.
options.why: A flat reply makes big news feel small.

options.text: No way!! That’s amazing, you totally deserve it. How did you find out?
options.reaction: Thank you!! My boss called me in and…
options.why: Excitement plus a question lets her relive the joy with you.

steps.prompt: Celebrate properly.
steps.why: Inviting more detail shows you genuinely want to share their happiness.

steps.prompt: How do you usually respond to others’ good news?
steps.reply: A little extra enthusiasm and a question can make their good news feel even better.

steps.body: When someone shares good news this week, respond with excitement and ask a question about it.

lessons.title: Join Their World
lessons.summary: Show interest in what they love, even if it’s not your thing.

steps.title: Visit their interests
steps.body: You don’t have to love fishing, gaming or gardening. But asking about it, or joining in once, shows you care about what makes them light up.

steps.prompt: Match their interest to a way to join in.

pairs.b: Ask them to show you a level

steps.why: A little curiosity about their world says “what matters to you matters to me”.

steps.prompt: Your partner is excited about a new board game. You’re not a games person. What’s best?

options.text: “Games are boring, but you go ahead.”
options.why: Dismissing it can make them feel their interest doesn’t matter.

options.text: “I’m not a gamer, but I’ll try one round with you!”
options.why: Joining in, even once, shows real interest in their joy.

options.text: Say nothing and leave the room.
options.why: Disappearing can feel like a lack of interest in them.

steps.prompt: Whose interests could you learn more about?
steps.reply: Even one question about it could mean more to them than you’d expect.

steps.body: Ask someone close to show or tell you about something they love, and give it your full attention.

lessons.title: Make a Weekly Ritual
lessons.summary: A small regular ritual gives you something to look forward to.

steps.title: Rituals anchor us
steps.body: Friday pizza, a Sunday walk or a weekly phone call are small rituals that build closeness. They don’t need to be fancy, just regular and shared.

steps.prompt: Good ritual idea, or just a chore?
steps.why: Rituals are about enjoying time together. Chores keep life running but rarely feel connecting.

steps.prompt: You’d love more time with your grown-up brother, but you’re both busy. What’s a good idea?

options.text: Wait until a big family event.
options.why: Waiting for rare events means long gaps between catch-ups.

options.text: Suggest a 15-minute call every Sunday evening.
options.why: Short and regular is easier to keep than long and rare.

options.text: Plan an expensive weekend away once a year.
options.why: Lovely, but a yearly treat doesn’t build everyday closeness.

steps.prompt: What ritual would you love to start?
steps.reply: Great choice. Suggest it this week and see who joins in.

steps.body: Suggest one small weekly ritual to someone close and agree on a day to start.

lessons.title: Hello and Goodbye
lessons.summary: How you greet and part from people matters.

steps.title: The bookends of the day
steps.body: A proper hello when someone comes home, and a warm goodbye when they leave, take seconds but make people feel valued. Looking up from your phone is a great start.

steps.prompt: Your partner comes home while you’re reading the news. What’s the most connecting response?

options.text: Keep reading and say “hi” without looking up.
options.why: A distracted hello can feel like they barely registered.

options.text: Put the phone down, smile and ask how their day was.
options.why: A few seconds of full attention makes them feel genuinely welcomed.

options.text: Start telling them about the news straight away.
options.why: Diving into your own topic skips over greeting them.

steps.prompt: Match the moment to a warm bookend.

pairs.b: “Have a great day, see you tonight!”

steps.why: Warm hellos and goodbyes frame the day with care. They’re tiny moments with big effects.

steps.prompt: How do you usually greet people at home?
steps.reply: Trying a warmer hello for a week could quietly change the feel of your home.

steps.body: This week, put your phone down and give a proper hello and goodbye to the people you live with.

lessons.title: Traditions That Fit
lessons.summary: Create traditions that suit who you are now.

steps.title: Make them your own
steps.body: Traditions don’t have to come from your family or match anyone else’s. A yearly picnic, an annual photo or a silly birthday song can become your own special thing.

steps.title: Planning something new

lines.text: Can you believe we’ve been friends for ten years?!
We should do something to mark it 🥳

steps.prompt: What do you suggest?

options.text: Let’s do it every year: same café, same day, one photo together!
options.why: A simple yearly tradition gives your friendship a special ritual to look forward to.

options.text: Eh, it’s just a number.
options.why: Brushing it off misses a lovely chance to celebrate together.

options.text: Maybe one day.
options.why: A vague maybe rarely turns into a real plan.

steps.prompt: Suggest a tradition.
steps.after: on the first day of spring?
steps.why: A simple, enjoyable activity is easy to repeat, which is what makes it a tradition.

steps.prompt: Which tradition would you love to start?
steps.reply: Lovely. Suggest it to someone and make this year the first one.

steps.body: Suggest one small tradition to someone you love and put the date in your calendar.

lessons.title: Thank the Everyday
lessons.summary: Thank people for the ordinary things they do.

steps.title: The unseen jobs
steps.body: Cooking dinner, sorting the bins or texting to check you got home are easy to overlook. Thanking people for the everyday things helps them feel seen and appreciated.

steps.prompt: Often overlooked, or usually thanked?

cards.text: Topping up the car with fuel

steps.why: Big gestures get thanks naturally. Everyday jobs deserve it too, and thanking them builds real warmth.

steps.prompt: Thank an everyday job.
steps.why: Naming the specific job shows you noticed something that often goes unseen.

steps.prompt: Which everyday job does someone do for you that you rarely thank?
steps.reply: A quick thank-you for that today could brighten their week.

steps.body: Thank someone today for an ordinary task they do, naming exactly what it was.

lessons.title: Say It in Writing
lessons.summary: A written thank-you can be kept and reread.

steps.title: Words they can keep
steps.body: A note in a lunchbox, a card or even a heartfelt message can be read again and again. Written thanks often means more because it can be kept.

steps.prompt: Your grandma knitted you a jumper. What would mean the most to her?

options.text: A quick “thanks” next time you see her.
options.why: Kind, but it might pass quickly and be forgotten.

options.text: A handwritten card about how cosy it is and when you wear it.
options.why: A specific, written thank-you is something she can keep and reread.

options.text: A thumbs-up emoji.
options.why: An emoji is easy to miss and doesn’t match the effort she put in.

steps.prompt: Order a heartfelt thank-you note.
steps.why: Naming the action and its impact makes the note specific. Ending warmly makes it feel personal.

steps.prompt: When did you last write someone a thank-you?
steps.reply: However long it’s been, a short note this week would be a lovely surprise.

steps.body: Write a short thank-you note or message to someone today, saying what they did and how it helped.

lessons.title: Thank Them in Public
lessons.summary: Praise in front of others can make people feel valued.

steps.title: Public appreciation
steps.body: Mentioning someone’s kindness in front of others, “Jo cooked this amazing meal”, lets them feel proud and appreciated. Just check they’re comfortable with attention first.

steps.prompt: Match the moment to some public appreciation.
steps.why: Sharing appreciation in front of others makes it feel even more meaningful to them.

steps.title: At a family gathering

lines.text: This garden looks wonderful! Who did all this?

steps.prompt: Your partner did most of it. What do you say?

options.text: Oh, we both did it.
options.why: Sharing the credit misses the chance to celebrate your partner’s work.

options.text: Thanks! (and change the subject)
options.why: Taking the compliment quietly overlooks who really did the work.

options.text: That was all Alex! They spent every weekend on it.
options.why: Giving them public credit makes them feel seen and appreciated.

steps.prompt: How do you feel about being praised in front of others?
steps.reply: Good to know. Others may differ, so a quick check on what they prefer helps.

steps.body: This week, mention something kind or impressive someone did while others are around, if they’re comfortable with it.

lessons.title: Play Together
lessons.summary: Play and fun are serious glue for relationships.

steps.title: Fun bonds people
steps.body: Laughing, playing games or being silly together releases tension and builds warm memories. Relationships need fun, not just serious talks and chores.

steps.prompt: Life has felt heavy lately with your family. What could help?

options.text: Wait until things calm down before having fun.
options.why: Waiting for a perfect moment can mean fun never happens.

options.text: Suggest a silly board game night this weekend.
options.why: A bit of play can lift the mood and bring everyone closer.

options.text: Plan a serious family meeting.
options.why: Talks have their place, but fun can reconnect you in a different way.

steps.prompt: Playful, or just routine?

cards.text: A water fight in the garden

steps.why: Playful moments create shared joy. Routine keeps life going, but play keeps it light.

steps.prompt: When did you last properly laugh with someone close?
steps.reply: If it’s been a while, a small dose of fun could be just what you both need.

steps.body: Plan one silly or playful thing to do with someone close this week, just for fun.

lessons.title: Try Something New
lessons.summary: New experiences together create fresh connection.

steps.title: Newness brings closeness
steps.body: Trying something new together, like a class, a new walk or a different recipe, creates excitement and shared memories. It reminds you how fun the other person can be.

steps.prompt: Match the usual plan to something new.
steps.why: Small changes to your usual plans can make time together feel fresh and exciting.

steps.prompt: Suggest something new.
steps.why: A new activity gives you something fun to learn and laugh about together.

steps.prompt: Your friendship has felt a bit samey lately. What’s a good idea?

options.text: Assume it’s just how friendships get.
options.why: Accepting it as normal means missing the chance to refresh things.

options.text: Suggest learning something new together, like climbing.
options.why: A shared new experience can add fresh energy to the friendship.

options.text: See each other less often.
options.why: Pulling back usually makes things feel even more distant.

steps.body: Suggest one new activity to try with someone close, and pick a date to do it.

lessons.title: Laugh It Off
lessons.summary: Gentle humour can ease tension and bring you closer.

steps.title: Laughter softens things
steps.body: Laughing together when things go wrong, like a burnt dinner or a missed train, can turn a stressful moment into a shared story. Just keep the humour kind, never at their expense.

steps.prompt: Kind humour, or unkind?

cards.text: Laughing together at a burnt cake

steps.why: Kind humour brings people together. Jokes at someone’s expense, even “just banter”, can hurt.

steps.title: A small disaster

lines.text: Soooo I may have set off the smoke alarm making toast 😅

steps.prompt: How do you reply?

options.text: Seriously? You can’t even make toast?
options.why: Mocking them turns a funny mishap into a put-down.

options.text: Chef of the year 😂 Shall I bring home some ready-made toast?
options.reaction: Haha, yes please, I’m banned from the toaster.
options.why: Gentle teasing that you both laugh at turns it into a shared joke.

options.text: Did you damage anything?
options.why: Practical, but it misses the chance to share a laugh.

steps.prompt: Who makes you laugh the most?
steps.reply: Tell them! Knowing they make you laugh is a lovely thing to hear.

steps.body: Find something to laugh about together with someone close today, keeping the humour kind.

lessons.title: Just Be There
lessons.summary: In hard times, your presence matters more than perfect words.

steps.title: Presence over perfection
steps.body: When someone is struggling, we often worry about saying the right thing. Usually, simply being there, sitting with them or saying “I’m here”, matters most.

steps.prompt: Your friend’s pet has just died. You don’t know what to say. What’s best?

options.text: Stay away until you think of the right words.
options.why: Waiting for perfect words can leave them feeling alone.

options.text: “I’m so sorry. I don’t know what to say, but I’m here.”
options.why: Honest and warm, it shows you care without needing the right words.

options.text: “At least you can get a new one.”
options.why: Trying to fix it quickly can make their grief feel dismissed.

steps.prompt: Offer your presence.
steps.why: It’s honest and reassuring, without pretending you can fix their pain.

steps.prompt: What makes it hard to be there for someone struggling?
steps.reply: All understandable. Remember, being there matters more than the perfect words.

steps.body: If someone you know is struggling, send a simple “Thinking of you, I’m here” message today.

lessons.title: Ask What Helps
lessons.summary: Different people need different support. Ask.

steps.title: Support isn’t one-size-fits-all
steps.body: Some people want to talk, some want distraction and some want practical help. Asking “What would help most right now?” lets you give the support they actually need.

steps.prompt: Match the need to a helpful offer.
steps.why: Matching support to their need makes it feel truly helpful rather than generic.

steps.title: A tough week

lines.text: Sorry I’ve been quiet. My dad’s in hospital.
Everything’s a bit much right now.

steps.prompt: What do you reply?

options.text: I’m so sorry. Would it help if I covered your Thursday meeting?
options.reaction: That would honestly be amazing. Thank you.
options.why: A specific, practical offer lightens their load in a real way.

options.text: Let me know if you need anything!
options.why: Kind, but vague offers are often hard for people to take up.

options.text: Hospitals are awful, my gran was in for weeks…
options.why: Sharing your story turns the focus away from them.

steps.prompt: When you’re struggling, what helps you most?
steps.reply: Knowing that about yourself makes it easier to ask others what they need too.

steps.body: Next time someone’s struggling, ask “What would help most right now?” before offering anything.

lessons.title: Keep Showing Up
lessons.summary: Support matters most after the first few days.

steps.title: The quiet after the storm
steps.body: When something hard happens, support pours in at first, then fades. Checking in weeks later, when others have moved on, can mean the most.

steps.prompt: Your friend’s divorce was finalised two months ago. What’s a caring move?

options.text: Assume they’re over it by now.
options.why: Big changes take time, and support often fades too soon.

options.text: “Thinking of you. How are you doing these days?”
options.why: A gentle check-in later shows you haven’t forgotten what they’re going through.

options.text: Avoid mentioning it so you don’t upset them.
options.why: Avoiding it can feel like nobody cares any more.

steps.prompt: Order long-term support.
items: Check in again after a month
steps.why: Support spread out over time catches people when others have stopped asking.

steps.prompt: Who might need a later check-in from you?
steps.reply: If someone came to mind, a short message today could mean a great deal.

steps.body: Think of someone who went through something hard a while ago, and check in on them today.

lessons.title: Small Daily Contact
lessons.summary: Little messages keep you close when you’re apart.

steps.title: Tiny threads of connection
steps.body: When you live apart or are busy, small daily messages, like a photo of your lunch or a quick “thinking of you”, keep a sense of togetherness alive.

steps.prompt: A small connecting message, or not?

cards.text: A photo of a dog that looks like theirs
“This song made me think of you.”

steps.why: Personal little messages say “you’re on my mind”. Generic or delayed ones don’t carry the same warmth.

steps.prompt: Send a little thread.
steps.why: A simple “thought of you” makes people feel remembered, even from far away.

steps.prompt: Who would love a little message from you?
steps.reply: Lovely. It only takes a moment, and it could make their day.

steps.body: Send a small, personal “thought of you” message to someone you don’t see often.

lessons.title: Share Your Day
lessons.summary: Telling each other the little things keeps you close.

steps.title: The little stuff matters
steps.body: Closeness grows from sharing ordinary moments: the funny thing on the bus, a tricky email, a lovely lunch. When apart, sharing these keeps you part of each other’s lives.

steps.title: Evening catch-up call
steps.prompt: What do you reply?

options.text: Fine, nothing much.
options.reaction: Oh, okay. Mine was fine too.
options.why: A flat answer gives them nothing to connect with.

options.text: A pigeon stole someone’s sandwich on my lunch break 😂 How was yours?
options.reaction: HAHA no way! Okay, mine was…
options.why: Sharing a small, funny moment invites them to share theirs too.

options.text: Busy. Gotta go.
options.why: Rushing off misses a chance to feel close.

steps.prompt: You and your partner are in different cities this week. What keeps you close?

options.text: Only message if something big happens.
options.why: Waiting for big news means missing the everyday moments that bond you.

options.text: Share a small highlight from each day.
options.why: Little daily highlights keep you part of each other’s lives.

options.text: Save everything for when you’re back.
options.why: By then, many moments will be forgotten or feel old.

steps.prompt: Do you usually share the little things?
steps.reply: The small things often matter most. Try sharing one a day.

steps.body: Share one small highlight from your day with someone you love, even if it seems trivial.

lessons.title: Plan the Reunion
lessons.summary: Something to look forward to keeps distance bearable.

steps.title: Anticipation helps
steps.body: Being apart is easier when you have a date to look forward to. Planning your next meeting, even months ahead, gives you both something happy to count down to.

steps.prompt: You miss your friend who moved abroad. What’s a good step?

options.text: Say “we should visit sometime!” and leave it there.
options.why: “Sometime” often never comes without a real plan.

options.text: Pick a month together and start looking at flights.
options.why: A real date turns missing them into something to look forward to.

options.text: Accept you’ll rarely see each other now.
options.why: Giving up can let a good friendship slowly fade.

steps.prompt: Make a real plan.
steps.why: Booking makes it real, which gives you both something definite to look forward to.

steps.prompt: Match the distance to a way to count down.

pairs.b: A shared countdown in your chat

steps.why: Counting down together keeps the excitement alive and the connection strong.

steps.body: Pick a date to see someone you miss, and send them a message to start planning it.

lessons.title: Go a Layer Deeper
lessons.summary: Ask a follow-up question to go beyond the surface.

steps.title: The second question
steps.body: The first answer is often on the surface. A gentle follow-up, “What made you choose that?” or “How did that feel?”, invites people to share more of themselves.

steps.prompt: Match the first answer to a deeper follow-up.
steps.why: Follow-up questions show real interest and help people open up more fully.

steps.title: A thoughtful chat

lines.text: I’ve been thinking about moving back to my hometown.

steps.prompt: What’s the best reply?

options.text: Ooh, what’s drawing you back there?
options.reaction: Honestly, I miss my family a lot lately…
options.why: A curious follow-up opened the door to what really matters to them.

options.text: Don’t, it’s so boring there.
options.why: Shutting it down stops them sharing their real feelings.

options.text: Cool.
options.why: A one-word reply misses the chance to go deeper.

steps.prompt: Who would you love to know on a deeper level?
steps.reply: A few gentle follow-up questions could take you there.

steps.body: In your next conversation, ask at least one follow-up question to go a little deeper.

lessons.title: Share Something Real
lessons.summary: Opening up a little invites others to open up too.

steps.title: Openness is catching
steps.body: When you share something real, a worry, a hope or something you find hard, people often feel safe to share too. Closeness grows when both people let their guard down a little.

steps.prompt: A new friend asks how you’re finding life lately. What helps you connect?

options.text: “All good, thanks!”
options.why: Fine for small talk, but it keeps things on the surface.

options.text: “Honestly, I’ve been a bit lonely since moving. How about you?”
options.why: Sharing something real, then asking back, invites a deeper conversation.

options.text: Tell them every detail of your hardest year.
options.why: Sharing too much too soon can feel overwhelming for a new friend.

steps.prompt: Real but right-sized, or too much too soon?

cards.text: Your full family history on a first coffee
Every detail of your last break-up straight away

steps.why: Right-sized openness invites closeness. Too much too soon can overwhelm, so share in layers.

steps.prompt: What do you find hardest to share?
steps.reply: That’s worth knowing. Sharing just a little of it with someone safe can feel freeing.

steps.body: Share one small, real thing about yourself with someone you trust, then ask about them.

lessons.title: Make It Safe to Open Up
lessons.summary: How you react decides whether they’ll share again.

steps.title: Handle it with care
steps.body: When someone shares something personal, your response matters. Thanking them, listening without judging and keeping it private makes them feel safe to share again.

steps.prompt: Order a caring response to someone opening up.
steps.why: Thanks and listening make them feel safe. Asking what they need and keeping it private build lasting trust.

steps.prompt: Your friend admits they’re struggling with anxiety. What’s the most caring response?

options.text: “Thank you for telling me. That sounds really hard. How can I support you?”
options.why: It honours their honesty and asks what support they’d like.

options.text: “Everyone gets anxious, you’ll be fine.”
options.why: Brushing it off can make them regret opening up.

options.text: “You should see a doctor.” and change the subject.
options.why: Advice can be useful, but jumping to it and moving on can feel dismissive.

steps.prompt: Honour their honesty.
steps.why: It shows you value their openness, which makes them more likely to share again.

steps.prompt: How do you react when someone opens up?
steps.reply: All natural responses. Starting with “thank you for telling me” is always a good first step.

steps.body: When someone opens up to you this week, start your response with “Thank you for telling me.”

lessons.title: Notice How They’ve Grown
lessons.summary: Tell people the ways you’ve seen them change and grow.

steps.title: Seeing their growth
steps.body: People change over time. Noticing and naming it, “You’re so much calmer than you used to be”, shows you’re still paying attention and celebrating who they’re becoming.

steps.prompt: Name their growth.
steps.why: Naming positive growth shows you see the effort they’ve put into changing.

steps.prompt: Match the change you’ve noticed to a warm comment.
steps.why: Noticing growth helps people feel seen as they are now, not just as they used to be.

steps.prompt: Your sister used to hate public speaking and just gave a great speech. What do you say?

options.text: “Remember when you used to panic?”
options.why: Bringing up the old fear can take the shine off her achievement.

options.text: “Nice speech.”
options.why: Kind, but it misses how far she’s come.

options.text: “You were brilliant! You’ve grown so much.”
options.why: It celebrates her now and acknowledges the journey she’s made.

steps.body: Tell someone close one way you’ve seen them grow, and how proud it makes you feel.

lessons.title: Dream Together
lessons.summary: Shared hopes for the future bond people together.

steps.title: A shared horizon
steps.body: Talking about things you’d love to do together, a trip, a project or a future plan, gives your relationship a sense of direction and excitement.

steps.title: A lazy Sunday

lines.text: If we could do anything next year, what would it be?

steps.prompt: What do you reply?

options.text: Don’t know, we can’t afford much anyway.
options.why: Shutting down the dream misses a chance to plan something exciting.

options.text: Ooh, learn to surf somewhere sunny! What about you?
options.reaction: Yes!! And I want to grow our own veg 🥕
options.why: Sharing a dream and asking back starts a fun conversation about your future.

options.text: Whatever you want.
options.why: Leaving it all to them means you miss dreaming together.

steps.prompt: A shared dream, or just a to-do?
steps.why: Dreams bring excitement and closeness. To-dos keep life running but don’t inspire in the same way.

steps.prompt: What’s one thing you’d love to do with someone special?
steps.reply: Share it with them! It might become your next adventure.

steps.body: Ask someone close: “If we could do anything together next year, what would it be?”

lessons.title: Keep Choosing Them
lessons.summary: Lasting closeness comes from choosing each other, again and again.

steps.title: Connection is a choice
steps.body: The closest relationships aren’t built by luck. They’re built by choosing each other in small ways every day: a question, a thank-you, a laugh, a kind message.

steps.prompt: Order a day full of small connection.
steps.why: Small, steady moments of connection through the day keep relationships close and warm.

steps.prompt: Life is busy and you feel a bit distant from a close friend. What’s the best first step?

options.text: Wait until life calms down.
options.why: Life rarely calms down on its own, and distance can grow.

options.text: Send a message suggesting a short catch-up this week.
options.why: One small step towards them rebuilds closeness quickly.

options.text: Assume the friendship is fading.
options.why: Assuming the worst can make you stop reaching out.

steps.prompt: Match the skill to a daily way to use it.
steps.why: Small daily habits turn these skills into a closer, warmer relationship over time.

steps.prompt: What have you learned most about connection in these lessons?
steps.reply: Wonderful. Keep choosing your people in small ways, and the closeness will keep growing.

steps.body: Choose one small way to connect with someone you love today, and do it before bedtime.
